lesson.title: Build a Python Calculator
lesson.goal: i wanna build a calc in python in vs cods

steps.title: Print a welcome message
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, add the line print("Simple Calculator") at the bottom, then save the file.

checks.label: print line for the welcome message

precision_checks.label: calculator.py contains the welcome print line

targets.caption: Click at the end of the file, on the line below the comment, and type print("Simple Calculator"), then save with Cmd/Ctrl+S.

hints: Put the cursor on a new line below the comment at the top of calculator.py. Scroll down if you need to.
Type print, then an opening bracket and a double quote. The text Simple Calculator goes between the quotes.
Make sure the line starts at the far left of the file (no indentation) and that you save the file before moving on.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the closing bracket or quote, which gives a SyntaxError when you run the script in step 2.
Typing Print with a capital P. Python is case-sensitive, so it must be lowercase print.
Using curly quotes (“ ”) copied from a web page instead of straight double quotes (").
Forgetting to save the file, so the editor shows a dot on the tab and the code is not on disk for the checks.

steps.title: Run your script
steps.instructions: In the VS Code terminal, run python calculator.py (or python3 calculator.py on Mac/Linux) and check that Simple Calculator appears.

checks.label: Terminal prints the Simple Calculator banner
Editor still shows the print line

targets.caption: Type this in the VS Code terminal (use python3 on Mac/Linux if python isn't found), then press Enter
This is the line from step 1 that should make Simple Calculator appear

hints: Open the terminal in VS Code with Ctrl+` (Cmd+` on Mac), then make sure you are in the same folder as calculator.py.
Type the command exactly as shown, then press Enter. If you get 'python is not recognized' or 'command not found', try python3 instead.
The output should be a single line: Simple Calculator. If you see nothing, check that calculator.py is saved (Ctrl+S / Cmd+S) before running.
common_mistakes: Running the command from the wrong folder, so Python says it can't find calculator.py. Check the folder in the terminal prompt or run ls (Mac/Linux) / dir (Windows).
Typos in the filename, such as calculator.pi or Calculator.py. File names are case-sensitive on Mac and Linux.
Forgetting to save calculator.py before running, so the terminal runs the old version.
Typing the command into the editor file instead of the terminal, which shows no output.
Using python when only python3 exists (or the reverse). Try the other one if the first fails.

steps.title: Write an add function
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, above the print line, define def add(a, b): that returns a + b, then add print(add(2, 3)) at the bottom.
steps.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

# (place above the existing print line)

# at the bottom of the file:
print(add(2, 3))

checks.label: add function is written in the

targets.caption: Type the def add(a, b): function here, above the print line
Type print(add(2, 3)) on a new line at the bottom of the file

hints: Start a new line below the comments and type: def add(a, b):. Press Enter, then indent the next line with four spaces.
Inside the function, type return a + b. The function gives back the sum of its two inputs.
Put print(add(2, 3)) at the very bottom, then save with Cmd+S (Mac) or Ctrl+S (Windows/Linux) and run python calculator.py in the terminal. You should see 5 below Simple Calculator.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the colon after def add(a, b) causes a SyntaxError.
The return line must be indented under def add; if it sits at the left margin, Python reports an IndentationError or the function will not return a value.
Writing return a - b or returning a print instead of return; the output must be 5.
Typing the print(add(2, 3)) line inside the function body instead of at the bottom of the file, so nothing prints.
Forgetting to save the file before running, so the terminal shows the old output or nothing new.

steps.title: Add the other operations
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, add subtract, multiply and divide functions below add, with divide returning "Cannot divide by zero" when b is 0.

checks.label: divide function is in the editor
zero check message is in the

precision_checks.label: subtract, multiply and divide are defined

targets.caption: Place your cursor on the blank line just below the add function and paste the new functions there, keeping them at the top level (no indentation).

hints: Leave one blank line after the add function, then type each new function at the same left margin as def add.
Each function body is indented by four spaces. The divide function has an if block nested inside it, so that block gets eight spaces before return.
divide must check b == 0 (two equals signs) before it divides. Return the message string as written, with the exact spelling 'Cannot divide by zero'.
common_mistakes: Typing the body lines with no indentation, which gives an IndentationError when you run the file.
Using a single = in if b = 0, which is an assignment and a syntax error in an if statement.
Forgetting the final return a / b in divide, so the function returns None for valid inputs.
Putting the new functions above add or inside it, so the file ends up with functions nested or out of order.
Mixing tabs and spaces, which VS Code shows as misaligned indentation.

steps.title: Ask the user for input
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, replace the test print(add(2, 3)) with code that reads two numbers using float(input(...)) and an operator using input("Operator (+, -, *, /): ").
steps.code:
num1 = float(input("First number: "))
num2 = float(input("Second number: "))
op = input("Operator (+, -, *, /): ")

checks.label: Operator prompt appears in the terminal

precision_checks.label: calculator.py reads two numbers as floats
script runs with piped sample input

targets.caption: Keep the welcome line, then replace the test print(add(2, 3)) with the input lines below it.

hints: Type the three lines under print("Simple Calculator"), indented at the left margin.
Each input() call waits for you to type something and press Enter; float() turns the number text into a decimal number.
The prompt text goes inside the quotes of input(...). Check that the parentheses and quotes are balanced.
common_mistakes: Leaving the old print(add(2, 3)) line in place, so the test still runs instead of asking the user.
Forgetting float() around input(), which leaves the numbers as text and breaks later math.
Missing a closing parenthesis or quote, which shows a SyntaxError in the terminal when you run the file.
Typing the operator prompt with different spacing or characters than the lesson, which makes the screen check fail.

steps.title: Choose the operation
steps.instructions: In calculator.py, add an if/elif chain that checks the operator, calls the matching function, and prints the result.

precision_checks.label: calculator.py has the operator if/elif chain
calculator.py has the elif for division
calculator.py has the fallback else branch

targets.caption: Type the if/elif chain below this comment, after your print line.

hints: Put the new code at the bottom of calculator.py, below the print("Simple Calculator") line, and keep it flush to the left edge.
Each branch needs a colon at the end of its if/elif/else line, and the lines under it must be indented by four spaces.
The chain uses the names operator, num1 and num2 from the input step, and add, subtract, multiply and divide from steps 3 and 4. If your names differ, change them to match your file.
common_mistakes: Using a single = instead of == in the comparisons, which causes a SyntaxError.
Forgetting the colon after an if, elif or else line.
Indenting the branch body inconsistently, so Python raises IndentationError.
Naming the operator variable differently from the one you read in the input step, so the chain never matches.
Calling a function name that does not match the def name from steps 3 and 4 (for example, sub instead of subtract).

steps.title: Try your calculator
steps.instructions: In the terminal, run python calculator.py and enter 8, 2 and / to see 4.0 printed.

checks.label: Editor shows the calculator.py file open

precision_checks.label: calculator.py still contains the welcome print

targets.caption: Save the file, then run it from the VS Code terminal (Terminal > New Terminal)

hints: Make sure calculator.py is saved (Ctrl+S or Cmd+S) before running it.
Open the terminal in VS Code with Terminal > New Terminal, then type python calculator.py and press Enter.
Answer each prompt in order: 8, Enter, then 2, Enter, then /, Enter. The result 4.0 appears on the next line.
common_mistakes: Running the command from a folder other than the lesson folder, so Python reports that calculator.py cannot be found. Check the terminal's path first.
Typing the numbers and operator on one line when the program asks for them one at a time.
Typing / with a space or a different symbol, which gives an error or a different result.
Running the file without saving it first, so the terminal runs an older version of the code.
